title: Meet Nigeria again
subtitle: Five places. Five different ways to see home.
intro: Follow water, city streets, cloth and high ground. Notice how places connect, then try putting them back on the map yourself. Take your time: every stop has a short story and an optional deeper look.
routeNote: The dashed line connects our stops. It is a learning journey, not a road itinerary.

natural-earth.name: Natural Earth: populated places, rivers and state boundaries
natural-earth.note: The atlas's existing map datasets. City pins are approximate centres; the Obudu pin indicates the plateau area rather than Obudu town.

lokoja.name: Kogi State Government — the confluence state

kano.name: Kofar Mata Dye Pits — craft background

altitude.name: UCAR Center for Science Education — the troposphere

rail.name: Nigerian Railway Corporation — network history and services
rail.note: The official site describes the Lagos–Ibadan railway and the wider network. Straight-line map distances are not railway or road distances.

ui.name: University of Ibadan — university background
ui.note: A place of learning is one entry into the city; it does not stand for every neighbourhood or resident.

stops.name: Lagos
stops.title: A city with water between its neighbourhoods
stops.story: Before you picture traffic, picture water. Lagos grew around islands, a lagoon and the Atlantic coast. A bridge or a boat journey is a reminder that the blue parts of a map can shape a city's daily life just as much as its streets.
stops.notice: Find the sea south of Lagos. Then follow the coast with your eyes: this is the edge of a much larger West African coastline.
deeper: A lagoon is a coastal body of water partly separated from the open sea. On a small world map its channels and islands can disappear. Zooming in changes the questions you can ask about a place.

Lagos is on Nigeria's south-western coast, near Benin. It is not Nigeria's capital: Abuja is inland. Keep both places in your mental map rather than letting the best-known city stand for the whole country.

Roads and railways connect the coast to inland cities. The Nigerian Railway Corporation describes its early Lagos–Ibadan line as 193 km; our map estimate between approximate city pins is shorter because it measures a straight line, not a railway alignment.
stops.memory: Lagos: lagoon and Atlantic coast, in the south-west.
stops.reflection: What journey across water would you like to make here?

tasks.question: Find Lagos among the five marked places.
tasks.hint: Look for the south-western stop nearest the Atlantic coast. Ibadan is a little farther inland.
tasks.explanation: Lagos is the coastal stop in the south-west. Ibadan lies farther north and inland.

tasks.question: Which pair belongs in your first mental picture of Lagos?
options: Desert dunes and an inland oasis
tasks.hint: Start with the water around the city, rather than its traffic.
tasks.explanation: Lagos sits around a lagoon and the Atlantic coast. This helps explain why islands, bridges and water routes matter.

tasks.question: Using the approximate Lagos and Ibadan pins, which straight-line distance is the better estimate?
tasks.hint: The two south-western pins are close on the national map. Think about the width of Nigeria before choosing.
tasks.explanation: The atlas pins are about 120 km apart in a straight line. A road or railway follows its own alignment, so its travelled distance is different.

connection.title: The map in an everyday journey
connection.text: Imagine choosing between a crossing and a longer journey around water. Where a bridge is placed can change which neighbourhood feels nearby. This is a question to explore on a detailed map, not a claim that every Lagos resident travels the same way.

stops.name: Ibadan
stops.title: The coast is only the beginning
stops.story: Move inland from Lagos to Ibadan. You are still in the south-west, but the lagoon is no longer the city's organising feature. Picture a city spreading across hills: homes, markets and places of learning connected to a wider region. Nigeria's urban story has many centres.
stops.notice: Compare the two south-western pins. Ibadan is north and a little east of Lagos. A small movement on a national map can take you into a different city landscape.
deeper: Ibadan is the capital of Oyo State. Its rise during the nineteenth-century Yoruba conflicts is part of the history behind today's settlement pattern; cities do not arrive on maps fully formed.

A national map helps you place the city. A street map would help you ask different questions: where people meet, how neighbourhoods connect, or which hill offers a view. Neither scale tells the whole story.
stops.memory: Ibadan: inland and north of Lagos, in Oyo State.
stops.reflection: Which part of a city helps you feel you know it: a market, a view, a campus, or a neighbourhood?

tasks.question: Find Ibadan, the inland south-western stop.
tasks.hint: Find Lagos first, then move a little north and east. The two close pins have leader lines to their exact map positions.
tasks.explanation: Ibadan is the inland stop just north-east of Lagos. Both are in the south-west; their relationship is a useful anchor.

tasks.question: From Lagos, which direction takes you towards Ibadan?
tasks.hint: Read the two pins: Ibadan is higher on the map and slightly to the right.
tasks.explanation: Ibadan lies north and a little east of Lagos. The map shows their positions, not a recommended road route.

tasks.question: Choose two clues that correctly place Ibadan.
tasks.hint: Compare Ibadan with Lagos and Kano on the map; choose both clues, then check.
tasks.explanation: Ibadan is inland from Lagos and in the south-west. These relative positions give you two anchors instead of a single memorised dot.

connection.title: A city you can meet through a campus
connection.text: A university, a market or a hilltop can become a personal anchor in a large city. The University of Ibadan offers one route into its life of learning. Which kind of place helps you remember a city: somewhere you studied, ate, watched a performance, or met a friend?

stops.name: Lokoja
stops.title: Two rivers, one meeting
stops.story: At Lokoja, the Niger and Benue meet. Trace each river upstream and the town becomes part of a much larger picture: water arriving from different directions, then continuing south through one connected system. A river junction can be a powerful way to remember a place.
stops.notice: Follow the Niger towards the north-west and the Benue towards the east. Their meeting makes the familiar Y in Nigeria's river map.
deeper: The Niger enters Nigeria from Niger Republic. The Benue arrives from Cameroon. Below their confluence, the combined flow continues towards the Niger Delta and the Gulf of Guinea.

A river basin links places that may look separate on a political map. Water, farming and flooding connect communities upstream and downstream. The map's state boundaries are only one way to divide the landscape.
stops.memory: Lokoja: the meeting of the Niger and Benue.
stops.reflection: What might two communities on the same river share, even if a state boundary separates them?

tasks.question: Find Lokoja, near the meeting of the two great rivers.
tasks.hint: Look near the middle of our five-stop map, east of Ibadan and south of Kano. Follow the rivers towards their meeting.
tasks.explanation: Lokoja is the central stop where the Niger and Benue meet. The river junction is a stronger clue than remembering a dot alone.

tasks.question: Which two rivers meet at Lokoja?
tasks.hint: One gives Nigeria its name; the other enters the country from Cameroon.
tasks.explanation: The Niger and Benue meet at Lokoja. Their combined flow continues south towards the Niger Delta.

tasks.question: Put these places in downstream order, starting at the river meeting.
tasks.hint: Start inland where the rivers meet, pass through the delta, then reach the sea. Tap each item in order.
tasks.explanation: Below Lokoja, the connected river system continues towards the Niger Delta and then the Gulf of Guinea. Political boundaries do not interrupt the downstream relationship.

connection.title: Follow a drop of water
connection.text: Picture rain entering a river far upstream. By the time that water passes Lokoja, it belongs to a system crossing several borders. Farming, fishing and river travel are local activities with a wider geographic setting. A basin is a useful way to connect places without ranking them.

stops.name: Kano
stops.title: Cloth can carry a city's history
stops.story: A piece of dyed cloth offers another way into Kano. Its long history of trade and textile work connects a northern city to skills, materials and routes beyond its walls. The Kofar Mata dye pits are one place to begin that story. Geography is also what people make and exchange.
stops.notice: Kano is the northernmost stop in this journey. Look back towards the coast: a country's connections run across its interior as well as along its edges.
deeper: Kano was one of the Hausa city-states and a trading centre connected to Saharan routes. Craft and commerce belong in its history alongside kingdoms and political boundaries.

Indigo dyeing is associated with the Kofar Mata dye pits. A short field note cannot represent every maker or neighbourhood. Let the map introduce the place, then seek out the people who can tell their own stories.
stops.memory: Kano: the northern stop, with a long story of trade and textile craft.
stops.reflection: Which craft from your own home tells a story about the people and places connected to it?

tasks.question: Find Kano, the northernmost of our five stops.
tasks.hint: Go furthest north among the five markers. Kano is well inland, north of Lokoja.
tasks.explanation: Kano is the northernmost stop in this journey. It is inland, far from Lagos's coastal setting.

tasks.question: Kano is far inland. Does that mean it cannot connect to coastal trade?
options: No. Land routes can connect inland cities, markets and ports
Yes. Only coastal cities can trade with other regions
Yes. State boundaries stop the movement of goods
tasks.hint: Think of a network of places rather than asking whether one city has its own coastline.
tasks.explanation: An inland city can connect to other cities and ports through land routes. This explains a geographic possibility; it is not a timetable or a claim that every route is operating.

tasks.question: Choose two things a map could help you investigate about an inland craft economy.
options: The exact skill of an individual maker
The taste of every local dish
tasks.hint: Choose questions about where things are and how places connect. A map cannot replace people’s own knowledge.
tasks.explanation: Maps can help explore market connections and transport distances. Understanding skill, taste and lived experience also needs people, observation and other sources.

connection.title: An inland city can still face outward
connection.text: A maker depends on more than a workshop: materials, customers, knowledge and transport connect a craft to other places. Indigo dyeing offers one way into Kano’s textile history. Treat it as an introduction, not a substitute for listening to the city’s makers and communities.

stops.name: Obudu highlands
stops.title: Nigeria rises here
stops.story: Turn south-east towards the highlands of Cross River State, near Cameroon. The Obudu Plateau offers a different first picture of Nigeria: ridges, slopes and high ground. Distance from the Equator is not the only influence on a place's climate. Height matters too.
stops.notice: Our pin marks the plateau area, not Obudu town. Compare it with Lagos: both are in southern Nigeria, but one is coastal and the other is high ground near the eastern border.
deeper: A plateau is an elevated area of land. The Obudu highlands are in Cross River State near Cameroon; the surrounding terrain is not represented by a single town-centre pin.

In the lower atmosphere, temperature generally decreases with height. This is a broad pattern, not a weather forecast: season, rainfall, wind and local conditions still matter. A map of relief can explain things a map of states cannot.
stops.memory: Obudu highlands: elevated country in Cross River, near Cameroon.
stops.reflection: Which Nigerian landscape would surprise someone who pictured the whole country as one kind of place?

tasks.question: Find the Obudu highlands, near Cameroon in the south-east of our map.
tasks.hint: Choose the easternmost of our five stops, near the border with Cameroon. This is the plateau-area pin, not Obudu town.
tasks.explanation: The Obudu highlands stop lies in Cross River State near Cameroon. Its pin represents the plateau area rather than the town.

tasks.question: Why might high ground feel cooler than nearby lowlands?
options: Temperature generally decreases with height in the lower atmosphere
Every place near Cameroon has the same weather
Southern Nigeria is outside the tropics
tasks.hint: Think about altitude, not just latitude.
tasks.explanation: Temperature generally decreases with altitude in the lower atmosphere. Local weather still varies; this is a geographic pattern, not a forecast.

tasks.question: Choose two maps that could help explain differences between coastal Lagos and the Obudu highlands.
tasks.hint: One map shows height; another shows atmospheric conditions or longer-term patterns.
tasks.explanation: Relief and weather/climate maps add information that a list of state names cannot. Altitude and local conditions help explain why two southern places need not feel the same.

connection.title: Change the map, change the question
connection.text: A state map places Obudu in Cross River’s South South geopolitical zone. A relief map shows high ground near the eastern border. “South South” is a regional label, not a precise compass bearing. Both maps can be useful without saying the same thing.

editorial.summary: Expanded everyday-life connections, comparison, map scale and downstream reasoning. Pins remain approximate. Illustrations are interpretive field notes.
editorial.scope: Five Nigeria stops; Ghana, Benin and Cameroon regional-anchor review. Other profiles remain on the editorial backlog.

revisions.reason: The scored question now tests inland connections rather than treating one craft reference as a complete account of the city. Earlier answers are retained as history; the new question starts fresh.
